records.title: Report on the sixth blind test of organic crystal structure prediction methods
records.core_idea: The sixth CSP blind test evaluated 25 submissions against five challenging targets (a near-rigid molecule, a polymorphic drug candidate with five forms, a chloride salt hydrate, a co-crystal, and a large flexible molecule). All experimental structures except one potentially disordered Z'=2 polymorph were generated by at least one method, showing CSP methods now extend to salts, hydrates, co-crystals, and larger flexible molecules. Ranking remains the core unsolved problem.
records.innovation: Moved from submitting only three predictions to ranked lists of up to 100 structures (plus a second re-ranked list), permitted pure re-ranking submissions, split salts/co-crystals into separate categories, and saw solid-state DFT usage jump from 2 to 12 submissions along with free-energy and MD-based ranking.

chunks.statement: Benchmark lattice-energy methods achieve only ~3-4 kJ/mol accuracy for absolute lattice energies (best quantum-chemical benzene calc ~1 kJ/mol), yet polymorph energy differences that must be resolved are far smaller, so successful rankings often rely on fortuitous error cancellation.
chunks.scope: vdW-inclusive DFT and quantum-chemical lattice-energy methods applied to organic molecular crystals
chunks.evidence: 'benchmark studies... suggest accuracies of 3-4 kJ/mol for absolute lattice energies, while one of the most sophisticated quantum-chemical calculations of the lattice energy of benzene is accurate to only 1 kJ/mol... accuracies of lattice-energy differences therefore may still involve fortuitous cancellation of errors'

chunks.statement: CSP success has two distinct requirements: (1) the experimental structure must correspond to a local minimum of the fitness function so it is GENERATED, and (2) it must be RANKED highly. Structures can be generated by the search but discarded during intermediate ranking before reaching accurate final ranking, causing failures unrelated to search coverage.
chunks.scope: all CSP workflows with hierarchical generate-then-rank pipelines
chunks.evidence: 'Experimental structures were initially generated by some search algorithms but not ranked highly by the intermediate optimisation and ranking methods, and therefore not brought forward to the final stages where these missing structures could have ranked highly.'

chunks.statement: Conformers that appear unstable or are saddle points for the isolated molecule in vacuo can be the ones adopted in the stable crystal; some may not even correspond to a gas-phase minimum. Rigid searches using gas-phase-favored conformers systematically miss experimental structures (seen acutely for XXVI, the largest/flexible target).
chunks.scope: flexible molecules with multiple accessible conformations in CSP
chunks.evidence: 'conformers that appear unstable for the molecule in vacuo can be found in the stable crystal structure... in some cases the solid-state conformation may not even correspond to a conformer on the isolated molecule's potential-energy surface'; XXVI failures 'attributed to difficulties in generating the experimental conformation due to its distorted nature'

chunks.statement: Force fields and even some vdW-DFT approximations can mispredict molecular conformation: for target XXII many methods flattened the hinged dithiino ring (a saddle point), traced to poor treatment of S atoms with some dispersion approaches, seeding wrong crystal structures even in fully ab initio submissions.
chunks.scope: molecules with soft internal degrees of freedom / heavy-atom vdW (S) treatment
chunks.evidence: 'Some force fields fail to adequately represent the hinge of this molecule... Even some DFT methods have difficulty with the conformation... traced back to issues treating the S atoms with some vdW approaches... a number of submissions, even fully ab initio ones, featured crystal structures with flat or nearly flat molecules'

chunks.statement: Finite-temperature free energies (harmonic Helmholtz Fvib) change polymorph rank order and repeatedly IMPROVED the ranking of experimental structures; use them when energy gaps between competitors are small. Free-energy/MD calculations cost >=1 order of magnitude more than the geometry optimization.
chunks.scope: polymorph ranking where lattice-energy gaps are small (e.g. XXII, XXIII)
chunks.evidence: 'The second lists of Day et al., Price et al. and Tkatchenko et al. all employed Helmholtz free energies, which changed the rank order... and, in all three cases, improved the ranking of the experimentally known structure'; 'the cost of all of these calculations is substantial, often more than an order of magnitude more than the initial geometry optimisation'

chunks.statement: 0 K equilibrium geometries inflate RMSD vs experiment because they omit thermal expansion and zero-point motion. For XXII an MD simulation at the true 150 K experimental temperature gave RMSD20 = 0.140 A, smaller than any submitted static structure; a 300 K MD gave 0.187 A.
chunks.scope: comparing predicted 0 K structures to finite-temperature diffraction structures
chunks.evidence: 'For XXII, MD simulations at 300 K gave an RMSD20 of 0.187 A... but a post-test MD simulation at the experimental temperature of 150 K, gives a value of 0.140 A, which is smaller than the RMSD values for the submitted structures. This demonstrates the significant contribution of thermal and zero-point motion to RMSDs.'

chunks.statement: Salt vs co-crystal is a fine and sometimes unresolvable line: target XXV, announced as a co-crystal, was later found proton-disordered (O occupancy 0.58, N 0.42) - a mixture of salt and co-crystal. Methods with fixed protonation states cannot explore this; only DFT-based rankings allowed barrierless proton migration to reveal salt forms.
chunks.scope: multi-component acid-base systems where proton position is ambiguous
chunks.evidence: 'the hydrogen-bonding proton in XXV is disordered, making the structure a mixture of a molecular salt and a co-crystal'; 'proton occupancies of 0.58 on the carboxylic acid oxygen and 0.42 on the nitrogen'; salt prediction 'possible due to their use of DFT in the final ranking stage, which allows for proton migration... only if there is no barrier'

chunks.statement: Computational cost and success are weakly correlated: for XXII some cheap empirical-potential + rigid-multipole submissions (<200 CPU hours) succeeded while several full DFT/ab initio submissions (orders of magnitude more cost) failed. Match method complexity to the physics that actually limits the target.
chunks.scope: CSP method selection across target difficulty levels
chunks.evidence: 'a few submissions predicted the known experimental structure with less than 200 CPU hours, using comparatively simple empirical potentials... Conversely, a number of full DFT/ab initio submissions for XXII failed to predict the experimental structure, despite using orders of magnitude more computational resources'

chunks.statement: Hierarchical ranking is standard: cheap potentials or coarse DFT (e.g. Harris-approximation charge densities) triage a large pool, then progressively expensive methods (bespoke multipole/DFT-fitted potentials, then full periodic vdW-DFT like PBE+MBD, TPSS-D3, PBE+XDM) rank the survivors near the global minimum.
chunks.scope: modern CSP ranking workflows (2016 blind test participants)
chunks.evidence: 'a hierarchical approach has been adopted, in which a less intensive computational method or algorithm is used initially... More computationally demanding methods and algorithms were then employed for the final set of structures closest to the global minimum'; 'Solid-state DFT calculations have been used by 12 submissions... where only two submissions employed DFT' in the fifth test

chunks.statement: A CSP landscape densely populated with low-energy putative structures near the global minimum signals likely polymorphism and unreliable single-structure prediction; large energy gaps above the minimum signal a robust prediction. Multiple submissions independently finding the same low-energy putative structures strengthens confidence that they are real candidate forms.
chunks.scope: interpreting energy landscapes to guide experiment rather than predict 'the' structure
chunks.evidence: 'For XXV, some of the submitted lists show large gaps in terms of energy... For other systems, the results show a range of structures close to the global minimum, which is more indicative of potential polymorphism'; 'many of the other structures predicted as being low in energy were found in multiple submissions'

records.synthesis: For GAtor 2.0, the sharpest lessons are about the generate/rank split and conformer handling. GA operators must sample crystal-relevant conformers, not just gas-phase minima (XXII/XXVI failures) - Genarris generation and mutation/crossover should preserve or explore in-crystal conformations, and any GA that relies on a cheap fitness for niching risks pruning a true structure before an accurate ranker (PBE0+MBD, MACE-OFF/AIMNet2/UMA) ever sees it, so the pool advanced from intermediate ranking should be generous. The 3-4 kJ/mol accuracy floor versus sub-kJ/mol polymorph gaps means GAtor's ranking layer should treat near-degenerate clusters as a set and, where gaps are tight, add harmonic free energies (which consistently helped here) rather than trusting static energy order. For multi-component/Z'>1 work, XXV warns that fixed protonation states blind you to salt/co-crystal disorder - run parallel neutral and charged searches and let a DFT/MLIP relaxation reveal proton migration. Finally, the cheap-beats-expensive result argues for MLIP-driven massive generation feeding selective DFT refinement, and the landscape-density heuristic gives GAtor a natural confidence metric: a flat, crowded low-energy basin means recommend more experiments, not one prediction.

records.title: GAtor: A First-Principles Genetic Algorithm for Molecular Crystal Structure Prediction
records.core_idea: GAtor is a massively parallel, first-principles genetic algorithm for molecular crystal structure prediction that uses dispersion-inclusive DFT (via FHI-aims) for local relaxations and energy evaluations, with molecular-crystal-specific breeding operators and machine-learning-based evolutionary niching to sample the potential energy surface broadly. Applied to four chemically diverse blind test targets, it recovered the experimental structures and other low-energy minima for all four.
records.innovation: Introduces evolutionary niching: machine learning clusters the dynamically updated population by structural similarity and a cluster-based fitness function evolves multiple subpopulations, counteracting initial-pool and selection biases (genetic drift). Combines this with molecular-crystal-tailored crossover/mutation operators and a hierarchical DFT re-ranking scheme, all driven directly by first-principles energies rather than force fields.

chunks.statement: Evolutionary niching promotes uniform sampling of the PES by evolving several subpopulations simultaneously, which helps overcome initial-pool biases and selection biases (genetic drift) that otherwise collapse a GA onto a few basins.
chunks.scope: GA-based molecular crystal structure prediction
chunks.evidence: Paper: 'Evolutionary niching promotes uniform sampling of the potential energy surface by evolving several subpopulations, which helps overcome initial pool biases and selection biases (genetic drift).'

chunks.statement: Clustering the dynamically updated population by structural similarity via machine learning and applying a cluster-based fitness function lets a GA reach disconnected, hard-to-reach regions of the energy landscape and locate numerous low-energy minima.
chunks.scope: GA molecular CSP with descriptor/ML-based similarity clustering
chunks.evidence: Paper: niching implemented 'by using machine learning to cluster ... population by structural similarity and then employing a cluster-based fitness function' increasing likelihood of 'locating numerous low-energy minima, including those located in disconnected, hard to reach regions.'

chunks.statement: GAtor performs the GA search with dispersion-inclusive DFT for local optimizations and energies, then re-relaxes and re-ranks the best generated structures with a hierarchy of increasingly accurate DFT functionals and dispersion methods.
chunks.scope: First-principles molecular CSP pipeline (GAtor + FHI-aims)
chunks.evidence: Paper: 'best structures generated are re-relaxed and re-ranked using a hierarchy of increasingly accurate DFT functionals and dispersion methods'; local optimizations/energies via FHI-aims with dispersion-inclusive DFT.

chunks.statement: Breeding operators designed specifically for molecular crystals provide a deliberate balance between exploration (diversity) and exploitation (refining good structures).
chunks.scope: GA operators for molecular crystals
chunks.evidence: Paper: 'Breeding operators designed specifically for molecular crystals provide a balance between exploration and exploitation.'

chunks.statement: Validate a CSP method on chemically diverse targets spanning different intermolecular interaction types; GAtor was benchmarked on four past blind test targets characterized by different interaction motifs and found the experimental plus other low-energy structures for all four.
chunks.scope: Benchmarking molecular CSP methods against CSP blind test targets
chunks.evidence: Paper: 'applied to a chemically diverse set of four past blind test targets, characterized by different types of intermolecular interactions. The experimentally observed structures and other low-energy structures are found for all four targets.'

chunks.statement: Predicted crystal energy landscapes can produce a top-ranked putative structure that is not the experimentally reported form and differs in Z' and packing motif, so the lowest-energy prediction should not be assumed to be the known experimental polymorph.
chunks.scope: Molecular CSP ranking; e.g. Target II 5-cyano-3-hydroxythiophene
chunks.evidence: Paper: for Target II the top-ranked putative structure is a Z'=2, P-1, scaffold-packing-motif structure 'which has not been reported previously.'

records.synthesis: For GAtor 2.0 this founding paper anchors the design philosophy you are extending: the GA's power comes not from raw sampling but from actively fighting genetic drift, and evolutionary niching (ML clustering of the live population + cluster-based fitness) is the mechanism that keeps subpopulations alive in disconnected basins. As you swap FHI-aims relaxations for MLIPs (MACE-OFF, AIMNet2, UMA) and Genarris-generated pools, remember that the niching and molecular-specific operators are orthogonal to the energy backend -- the descriptors driving clustering are what preserve diversity, so descriptor choice directly controls whether niches map to real polymorph basins. The Target II result (a novel top-ranked Z'=2 structure) is a concrete reminder relevant to your Z'>1 and multi-component work: the GA readily finds low-energy putative forms that are not experimentally observed, so ranking fidelity (PBE0+MBD, and ultimately finite-temperature free energies) is where predictions live or die, not in generation coverage.

records.title: Genarris: Random generation of molecular crystal structures and fast screening with a Harris approximation
records.core_idea: Genarris generates random molecular crystal structures of rigid molecules under physical constraints (symmetry, cell parameters, close-contact checks), then screens them cheaply using a Harris approximation (superposition of single-molecule densities evaluated with dispersion-inclusive DFT without self-consistency). Machine-learning clustering with a purpose-built relative coordinate descriptor (RCD) plus affinity propagation drives selection into three workflows (Diverse, Energy, Rigorous) tailored to different goals, including seeding genetic algorithms.
records.innovation: First application of the Harris approximation to molecular-crystal configuration-space screening (fragments = whole molecules), implemented in FHI-aims with Wigner-matrix basis rotations. Introduces the relative coordinate descriptor (RCD) capturing relative positions/orientations of neighbor molecules rather than interatomic distances, and pairs it with affinity propagation clustering to resolve packing motifs and under-sampled regions.

chunks.statement: The Harris approximation (superposition of self-consistent single-molecule densities, energy evaluated without a self-consistency cycle) is accurate for weakly interacting molecules but fails when densities overlap; because it is non-variational, its binding-energy error is always negative and grows asymptotically as molecules get closer.
chunks.scope: Rigid molecular crystals/dimers of small organics in the van der Waals regime; PBE+TS@Harris
chunks.evidence: HA 'becomes exact when the molecules are far apart'; near equilibrium |dBE| small (0.0740, 0.0049, 0.0288 eV for targets II, XIII, XXII); 'Because of the non-variational nature of the HA, dBE(x) is always negative and its magnitude increases asymptotically with decreasing distance.'

chunks.statement: Harris-approximation binding energies and rankings agree remarkably well with self-consistent PBE+TS for randomly generated crystal pools, with r^2 for binding energies of 0.946-0.994 and for rankings 0.976-0.989 across close-contact settings.
chunks.scope: 2000-structure P21/n pools of Target XXII (nitrile-containing molecule), Z=4/Z'=1, sr = 0.500/0.625/0.750

chunks.statement: Set the close-contact cutoff (sr, fraction of summed vdW radii) in an intermediate window: too small admits unphysically close contacts that produce large negative HA errors, too large makes structures energetically too similar for the HA to resolve. An sr around 0.8-0.9 (or ~0.625 tuned) balances physicality against HA reliability and motif diversity.
chunks.scope: HA-screened random pools of rigid small organics
chunks.evidence: sr 'should be large enough to avoid unphysical structures... and small enough to allow for a diversity of crystal packing motifs'; default half-normal sr with bounds 0.9/0.05/0.8; sr=0.500 outliers had N...N contacts of 1.64, 1.80, 1.56 A; sr=0.750 pool too close in energy for HA to resolve.

chunks.statement: A descriptor based on relative positions and orientations of neighboring molecules (RCD) captures crystal packing motifs (correlating with space-group symmetry) better than atom-distance descriptors like the RDF, which instead track unit-cell volume; RCD also better identifies pre-relaxation near-duplicates.
chunks.scope: Rigid molecule crystals; comparison on 5000-structure raw pool of Target II
chunks.evidence: RCD shows 'stronger correlation with space group symmetry' and 'weaker correlation with the unit cell volume' than RDF; RCD-AP 'grouped almost all the duplicate pairs together up to 7 clusters'; RCD consistently higher silhouette scores, increasing with cluster number while RDF's decrease.

chunks.statement: Affinity propagation clustering resolves small, isolated, under-sampled regions of configuration space as distinct clusters (unlike k-means which merges satellite regions), and does so deterministically without a preset cluster count. This corrects sampling bias against rarely-generated packing motifs.
chunks.scope: Clustering of crystal-structure pools / synthetic 2D-3D test data
chunks.evidence: 'While k-means groups three of the satellite regions together into one cluster, AP successfully identifies them as distinct clusters'; AP identified a distinct low-a cluster containing structures within 0.2 eV of the global minimum; AP 'does not depend on a randomized initialization'.

chunks.statement: Genarris workflows apply hierarchical screening: generate a large raw pool (5,000-10,000), evaluate energies (HA for Diverse/Energy, self-consistent DFT for Rigorous), then alternate RCD-AP clustering with energy-based selection, reducing to ~1% final pool and fully relaxing only at the end. Diverse selects cluster exemplars for maximal spread; Energy over-clusters to concentrate on low-energy basins; Rigorous iterates cluster/select/partial-relax down to 5% then energy-selects.
chunks.scope: Genarris Diverse/Energy/Rigorous workflows for rigid molecules, Z=4/Z'=1
chunks.evidence: Raw pools of 5,000 (II, XIII) and 10,000 (XXII); 'each step of the Diverse and Energy workflows reduces the pool to 10%'; final pool 1% of raw; Rigorous repeats until pool <5%, then purely energy-based selection to 1%; full relaxation only for final pools.

chunks.statement: To seed a genetic algorithm, prefer a maximally diverse initial population over a low-energy one: the Diverse pool gave the best GA convergence to representative low-energy motifs and consistently found the experimental structures, while Energy-seeded runs were inconsistent and Random-seeded runs performed worst.
chunks.scope: GAtor genetic-algorithm runs on Targets II, XIII, XXII from Genarris pools
chunks.evidence: 'starting the GA from the Diverse pool results in the best performance... consistently find the experimental structures'; Energy pool 'leads to inconsistent performance'; Random pools 'consistently exhibit the worse performance'. 'We recommend using the Diverse workflow of Genarris to produce initial pools for GAtor.'

chunks.statement: Energy-selective screening over-samples low-energy basins, increasing the chance that similar structures relax into the same minimum (more post-relaxation duplicates) and leaving high-energy but distinct packing motifs under-sampled; the HA's largest ranking errors also occur precisely in the low-energy region that energy selection emphasizes, degrading r^2 step-to-step.
chunks.scope: HA-ranked energy-selective workflows for rigid small organics
chunks.evidence: Energy workflow 'tends to yield a higher number of duplicates' (e.g., 26 and 28 dup pairs for II and XXII); 'Energy and Rigorous workflows under-sample or completely miss certain clusters... tend to be higher in energy'; 'In the Energy workflow r^2 deteriorates significantly... where the errors of the HA are most severe.'

chunks.statement: van der Waals-dominated molecular crystals have many near-degenerate local minima, so accurate polymorph ranking demands energy resolution of a few meV; dispersion-inclusive DFT (especially many-body dispersion with hybrid functionals) is the de facto standard for final ranking, while generic force fields perform poorly.
chunks.scope: Molecular crystal structure prediction generally (CSP blind tests)
chunks.evidence: 'weak van der Waals interactions... lead to many local minima that are extremely close in energy, requiring energy resolution of a few meV'; 'Generic force fields have consistently been demonstrated to produce poor results'; MBD with hybrid functionals 'shown to be highly accurate'.

records.synthesis: For GAtor 2.0, the central lesson is that initialization diversity beats initialization depth: seed the GA from a maximally spread pool (Genarris Diverse) so niching/crossover can reach distinct packing motifs, rather than pre-committing to HA-ranked low-energy basins where the cheap energy method is least reliable and where duplicate collapse is worst. The RCD-AP machinery is directly reusable as a niching/duplicate-detection metric in the GA itself, since RCD tracks packing motifs (space-group-like) rather than cell volume and cleanly isolates rare, under-sampled funnels that random generation and energy selection both miss. When swapping the HA screening layer for modern MLIPs (MACE-OFF, AIMNet2, UMA), keep the same discipline: enforce physical close-contact filters (the HA's failure mode maps onto MLIP extrapolation errors on overlapping densities), reserve expensive PBE0+MBD and finite-temperature free-energy corrections for the final ~1% pool, and remember that ranking errors concentrate in the near-degenerate low-energy window that ultimately decides polymorph order.

records.title: Genarris 2.0: A random structure generator for molecular crystals
records.core_idea: Genarris 2.0 is an MPI-parallelized random molecular crystal structure generator that builds physically reasonable structures across all 230 space groups (general and special Wyckoff positions), using a machine-learned solid-form volume predictor, hierarchical intermolecular distance checks, and hydrogen-bond-aware cutoffs, followed by clustering/energy-based down-selection to produce a curated pool for CSP.
records.innovation: Versus the original Genarris: MPI/mpi4py parallelization with FHI-aims run inside sub-communicators, a topological-fragment ML model for solid-form volume estimation trained on the CSD, systematic generation on special Wyckoff positions via molecular-axis/viewing-direction alignment, a three-stage hierarchical structure-check scheme (including rigorous non-orthogonal minimum-image via sphere decoding), and element-specific hydrogen-bond cutoff distances.

chunks.statement: Solid-form volume (density) of a molecule varies across polymorphs with a standard deviation of ~2.95% - this sets a floor on how accurately any volume-estimation model can predict a specific polymorph's cell.
chunks.scope: Homomolecular organic crystals at room temperature/standard pressure; 2,173 unique polymorph pairs from the 2017 CSD
chunks.evidence: 'The distribution has a standard deviation of 2.95% with respect to the solid form volume of the molecule... places a lower bound on the expected accuracy of estimated solid form molecular volumes.'

chunks.statement: A raw van der Waals sphere Monte Carlo volume underestimates true solid-form volume by a factor of ~1.47; a plain linear correction gives ~4.72% error, but adding topological-fragment features reduces error to ~2.93%, matching the polymorph density spread.
chunks.scope: Chemically diverse CSD dataset, molecules 5-260 atoms spanning H,C,N,O, halogens, B,P,S,Si,Te,Se
chunks.evidence: 'the ratio... was found to be 1.47... standard deviation of 4.72% error... the fragment based model achieves an error of similar magnitude to the volume differences between polymorphs... sigma = 2.93%'

chunks.statement: About 70% of molecular crystals have molecules on general Wyckoff positions; the rest sit on special positions, most commonly two-fold axes (2), mirror planes (m), and inversion centers (bar-1).
chunks.scope: CSD-wide analysis of molecular crystals (Pidcock et al.)
chunks.evidence: 'in 70.1% of the molecular crystals, molecules occupy general positions, and in the remaining structures molecules occupy special positions. Among the special positions, two-fold rotation (2), mirror planes (m), and inversion centers are the most frequent.'

chunks.statement: Standard vdW cutoffs (0.85 x sum-of-radii) wrongly reject structures with strong X-H...Y hydrogen bonds because real H-bond contact distances are much shorter than typical vdW contacts; N/O donor-acceptor pairs need dedicated shorter cutoffs (effective sr ~0.55-0.62), while C-donor and halogen H-bonds are fine at 0.85.
chunks.scope: Homomolecular crystals with O-H/N-H donors to O/N acceptors; cutoffs from CSD IsoStar distributions
chunks.evidence: 'the sum of the vdW radii multiplied by the default sr value of 0.85... exceeds a large number of non-bonded interaction distances... Using the default sr value, structures with strong hydrogen bonds, such as glycine, would be deemed unphysical'; Table 2 gives sr 0.55-0.62 for OH/NH...O/N.

chunks.statement: The generation loop is: estimate solid-form volume (relax single molecule + ML model) -> find compatible space groups within a symmetry tolerance -> per space group draw a cell volume from a Gaussian (mean = predicted volume, sigma = 3x prediction error) -> build random cell, place/orient molecule (random for general positions, axis-aligned for special positions) -> apply symmetry ops -> hierarchical distance checks -> add passing structures to raw pool.
chunks.scope: Genarris 2.0 raw-pool generation for semi-rigid molecules with no rotatable bonds
chunks.evidence: 'A random volume is drawn from a Gaussian distribution whose mean and standard deviation are the predicted volume and three times the prediction error... The space group symmetry operations are then applied... The attempted structures that pass the intermolecular distance checks... are added to the raw pool.'

chunks.statement: Structure checking is done in three escalating stages to control the O(N^2) cost: Stage I ignores periodicity and uses center-of-mass/molecule-length screening (kills most bad structures cheaply), Stage II does approximate minimum-image distances in fractional coordinates after lattice reduction, and Stage III applies a rigorous sphere-decoder closest-vector solution only for the few non-orthogonal structures that survive.
chunks.scope: Genarris 2.0 close-contact detection, including triclinic/oblique cells
chunks.evidence: 'Genarris 2.0 performs a series of three hierarchical structure checks. Failed structures are discarded at each stage... most of the unphysical structures generated are rejected at this stage [I]... only few non-orthogonal structures that pass Stage I and Stage II reach Stage III. Hence, the overall efficiency is not compromised.'

chunks.statement: Space groups with glide planes and screw axes are easier to populate than those with mirror planes, because mirror-related molecules can overlap with their own mirror image; this biases which space groups are readily sampled even when a uniform distribution is targeted.
chunks.scope: Random generation of rigid molecular crystals; illustrated for benzene Z=4 and glycine Z=4
chunks.evidence: 'space groups like P2/m (10), Pmm2 (25), and Pmmm (47) which have mirror planes are harder to generate as molecules that touch the planes overlap with their own mirror image. In contrast, space groups with glide planes and screws axes are easier to generate because symmetry-equivalent molecules are translated in space.'

chunks.statement: Volume models trained on ambient-pressure CSD structures systematically over-predict cell volumes for high-pressure polymorphs; expect the predicted volume to be far from experiment when the target forms under pressure.
chunks.scope: Benzene high-pressure Z=2 (P2_1/c) polymorph at 25 kbar vs ambient-trained model
chunks.evidence: 'Our prediction for Z = 4 is much closer to the experimental volume than for Z = 2 because the latter forms under pressure of 25 kbar whereas the volume estimation model was trained on structures obtained under ambient pressure.'

chunks.statement: Unconstrained relaxation of pool structures can break or create symmetry, changing the apparent space group, Z, or Z', so the space group of a raw structure is not a reliable label for the relaxed structure.
chunks.scope: DFT geometry optimization (PBE+TS, no lattice constraints) of glycine/benzene pools
chunks.evidence: 'Relaxation of the final pool may break existing symmetries or create new ones as there are no constraints imposed. This resulted in additional space groups with a different Z or Z'. For example, space group Cmc2_1 (36) and space group P1 were created after geometry optimization for glycine with Z = 2.'

chunks.statement: Use the Robust down-selection workflow (RCD or RDF descriptor -> affinity-propagation cluster to ~10% -> single-point PBE+TS energies -> AP cluster again to ~10% keeping lowest-energy per cluster -> full relaxation) to produce a small, diverse, low-energy initial population rather than to guarantee finding the experimental structure.
chunks.scope: Genarris 2.0 curated-pool generation feeding downstream search (e.g., genetic algorithms)
chunks.evidence: 'the goal of the Robust workflow is not necessarily to find the experimental structure but to produce an initial population for a structure search algorithm, such as a genetic algorithm.' Default cluster count is 10% of the pool; workflow uses AP clustering then energy-based selection then relaxation.

records.synthesis: For GAtor 2.0, Genarris is the front end that seeds the initial GA population, so its biases become the GA's starting biases. Three lessons transfer directly: (1) The ML volume predictor's ~3% floor and its ambient-pressure training bias mean the initial cell volumes for high-pressure or unusually dense targets will be off - worth widening the volume-sampling sigma or seeding hand-built cells when chasing such polymorphs. (2) The special-Wyckoff generation and glide/screw-vs-mirror sampling bias matter for niching: if you want diversity across space groups (and for Z'>1 or high-symmetry molecules like benzene), you must actively ensure special positions and mirror-plane groups are represented, because random generation under-samples them and energy selection can further prune them. (3) Symmetry can change under relaxation, so any GA fingerprint/niching scheme keyed on space group should re-detect symmetry post-relaxation rather than trust the generated label. Finally, the H-bond cutoff insight is a practical reminder that for strongly H-bonded systems (amino acids, pharmaceuticals) generic vdW filters throw away the very dense, physically correct structures the GA needs in its gene pool.

records.title: Genarris 3.0: Generating Close-Packed Molecular Crystal Structures with Rigid Press
records.core_idea: Genarris 3.0 generates random molecular crystal structures in all compatible space groups (Z'=1) and introduces the 'Rigid Press' algorithm, which uses a regularized, differentiable hard-sphere potential to compress the unit cell into a close-packed arrangement based purely on geometry, with no energy evaluations. It is coupled to a clustering-and-down-selection workflow using MLIPs (MACE-OFF23(L)) in early stages and dispersion-inclusive DFT (PBE+MBD) for final ranking, and was demonstrated on six chemically diverse targets.
records.innovation: The Rigid Press geometric close-packing algorithm (regularized hard-sphere potential, symmetry-preserving, ~2 orders of magnitude cheaper than MLIP relaxation), combined with a diversity-preserving affinity-propagation clustering and multi-structure-per-cluster selection workflow that mitigates inaccurate MLIP energy rankings; also a systematic assessment of general-purpose MACE-OFF transferability across chemistries including energetic materials.

chunks.statement: Energy differences between molecular crystal polymorphs are usually only a few kJ/mol, which is what demands high-accuracy ranking methods.
chunks.scope: Molecular crystal polymorphs in general (CSP context)
chunks.evidence: 'the energy differences between polymorphs are usually only a few kJ/mol, requiring high accuracy.' In results, aspirin Form II vs Form I differ by 0.69 kJ/mol (PBE+MBD, 0 K); putative EM structures lie 2.69 kJ/mol (CL-20) and 1.69 kJ/mol (DNI) above experimental forms.

chunks.statement: A regularized hard-sphere potential can drive close packing purely geometrically: freezing internal molecular geometry and optimizing lattice vectors, molecular positions and orientations to minimize cell volume subject to intermolecular distance penalties reproduces near-experimental unit cell volumes without any energy evaluation.
chunks.scope: Rigid, single-conformer molecules, Z'=1, all space groups; demonstrated on 6 targets including H-bonded, van der Waals, and energetic crystals
chunks.evidence: Rigid Press minimizes F(s)=V(s)+P_contact(s) with piecewise differentiable penalty; after Rigid Press, cell volumes are close to experimental (slightly underestimated for aspirin/Target XXII/Target I; very close for dense delta-HMX and DNI). Matches to experiment appear for all targets only after Rigid Press.

chunks.statement: Pre-optimize randomly generated structures with Rigid Press before MLIP/DFT relaxation: it costs up to 2 orders of magnitude less than MLIP relaxation and sharply reduces the number of downstream relaxation steps, and for some targets a match to the experimental structure is only found when Rigid Press is used.
chunks.scope: CSP workflows relaxing thousands to millions of putative structures
chunks.evidence: 'The computational cost of Rigid Press optimization is lower by up to 2 orders of magnitude than relaxation using MLIPs.' For epsilon-CL-20, a match to experiment can only be found with Rigid Press (SI). SI Fig S1 shows Rigid Press pre-optimization reduces MACE-OFF relaxation steps.

chunks.statement: The Genarris 3.0 CSP down-selection pipeline runs: generate ~4000 structures per compatible space group at 1.5x inflated volume -> Rigid Press compression -> loose-tolerance duplicate removal per space group -> MACE-OFF SPE + affinity-propagation clustering to 10% -> MACE-OFF full relaxation + duplicate removal -> AP cluster to 100, keep up to 5 within 10 kJ/mol per cluster -> PBE+MBD SPE + AP cluster (keep all within 10 kJ/mol) -> final PBE+MBD relaxation + duplicate removal.
chunks.scope: Genarris 3.0 CSP workflow, Z'=1; thresholds are user-tunable
chunks.evidence: Detailed workflow in Methods: s_r=0.95 proximity check for generation, Rigid Press default s_r=0.85, StructureMatcher tolerances 0.5/0.5/10deg; AP clustering to 10% then 100 clusters; 10 kJ/mol windows; PBE+MBD final relaxation Tier 2 tight, 3x3x3 k-grid.

chunks.statement: When selecting survivors from clusters in a hierarchical CSP workflow, keep multiple low-energy structures per cluster (e.g., up to 5 within a 10 kJ/mol window) rather than only the single lowest-energy structure, because an inaccurate MLIP can rank the true structure poorly and a strict energy cutoff would discard it.
chunks.scope: Hierarchical CSP with general-purpose MLIP early-stage ranking, especially chemistries far from training data (energetic materials)
chunks.evidence: For DNI the experimental structure is ranked #79 (19.3 kJ/mol above min) by MACE-OFF but becomes the global minimum at PBE+MBD SPE; it survives because it is 2nd in its cluster and up-to-5-within-10-kJ/mol selection is used. Procedure especially benefits delta-HMX and epsilon-CL-20.

chunks.statement: General-purpose MLIPs (MACE-OFF23(L)) give strongly chemistry-dependent accuracy: excellent for drug-like molecules (aspirin, Target I) but markedly worse for chemistries underrepresented in training (Target XXII and especially energetic materials with nitrogen-rich groups), degrading both geometry relaxation and energy ranking.
chunks.scope: MACE-OFF23(L) trained on SPICE 1.0 (drug-like molecules); molecular crystal relaxation and ranking vs PBE+MBD
chunks.evidence: Relaxation match rates (RMSD30<1A): aspirin 86.6%, Target I 91.0%, Target XXII 80.2%, epsilon-CL-20 73.7%, delta-HMX 61.8%, DNI 56.9%. Ranking MAE/RMSE: <5 kJ/mol and Kendall >0.7 for aspirin/Target I; 9-13 kJ/mol and Kendall 0.5-0.6 for Target XXII/CL-20/DNI; >20 kJ/mol and Kendall <0.4 for delta-HMX. Experimental structure misranked as #12 (HMX), #8 (CL-20), #19 (DNI) by MACE-OFF.

chunks.statement: Dispersion-inclusive DFT remains indispensable for final ranking; validate general-purpose MLIP performance per system, and if inadequate, train a system-specific potential (e.g., AIMNet2) rather than trusting out-of-the-box MLIP energies.
chunks.scope: CSP energy ranking; especially chemistries far from MLIP training data
chunks.evidence: A system-specific AIMNet2 for CL-20 gives higher match rate, lower RMSD30, lower energy MAE and higher Kendall vs PBE+MBD than MACE-OFF, ranking the experimental structure #4 at 2.50 kJ/mol above minimum. Authors 'suggest exercising caution' and recommend case-by-case validation.

chunks.statement: Highly constrained (high-symmetry) space groups reduce the configurational degrees of freedom, making the correct structure easier to generate randomly, but also produce more symmetry-equivalent duplicates; a large fraction of duplicates signals exhaustive sampling of that space group.
chunks.scope: Random structure generation across space groups with special Wyckoff positions, Z'=1
chunks.evidence: delta-HMX (P6_1) yielded 268/52,573 matches at initial generation vs 0-1 for other targets; after generation duplicate removal reduces pools by factors of 5-20 (largest 19-20 for Target I and delta-HMX). High-symmetry/centered groups (e.g., Cm, Nos. 75-81) generate more duplicates.

chunks.statement: Relative stability of near-degenerate polymorphs can invert between 0 K lattice energy and finite-temperature free energy, so finite-temperature (e.g., QHA) corrections are needed when two forms are within ~1 kJ/mol.
chunks.scope: Near-degenerate polymorphs (aspirin Forms I and II), dispersion-inclusive DFT
chunks.evidence: PBE+MBD at 0 K ranks Form II below Form I by 0.69 kJ/mol, but PBE+MBD QHA free energy at 300 K predicts Form I more stable than Form II by 1.10 kJ/mol, consistent with experiment; prior studies note relative stability depends on method and free-energy corrections.

records.synthesis: For GAtor 2.0, Genarris 3.0's Rigid Press is the natural upstream partner: seeding the GA's initial population with geometrically close-packed, symmetry-consistent structures should improve the quality and diversity of the parent pool while cutting expensive relaxation steps, and its pure-geometry nature makes it a cheap 'repair' operator that GA offspring could be passed through before energy evaluation. The affinity-propagation-plus-multiple-per-cluster selection philosophy directly informs GA niching: keeping several low-energy members within an energy window per structural niche guards against a noisy fitness surrogate (an MLIP) prematurely purging the true global minimum - a real risk given the paper's demonstration that MACE-OFF misranks energetic-material structures by 8-19 positions. The central cautionary lesson for GAtor's fitness function is that a general-purpose MLIP's error is chemistry-dependent and can exceed the entire polymorph energy spread (a few kJ/mol), so for targets outside SPICE-like drug chemistry (energetic materials, unusual heteroatom motifs, Z'>1 or multi-component systems) the group should validate against PBE+MBD/PBE0+MBD, use system-specific AIMNet2 potentials, and reserve dispersion-inclusive DFT for final ranking. Finally, the aspirin 0 K/300 K inversion is a reminder that GA rankings and reported landscapes near degeneracy should be treated as provisional until finite-temperature (QHA) corrections are applied.
